beats.act: the game, the state, the object
beats.narration_text: Walker Rudy is a 2D side-scroller in Godot four point seven, on the Compatibility renderer. The state this assignment shows is Rudy's invulnerability: for one point two seconds after a hit, or after he gets back up, hits are ignored. While that window is open, the hearts in the corner tint toward the waystone's pale blue. The textured shader is in the 3D props scene, in Forward Plus, on two surfaces: the waystone's stone, and the teleport circle's dark inner disc.

shot.observation: Two frames from the film's own Movie Maker captures at a2a3a77: the 2D game three frames after hit 1 (two full hearts, one empty, Rudy knocked back and see-through), and the 3D props scene from its own camera with the textured waystone and circle.

qc.contrast_reason: Engine captures fill most of this card; the whole-frame ink average measures them, not text. The title is measured locally.

beats.narration_text: Four questions run through this film, and each answer points at a line. What a shader does: line eight of the tint shader. How a material differs from a shader: a material file that names the shader it uses. Why a texture is information: a sampler that reads directions, not colours. And what Godot's shading language is: words like group uniforms, which plain GLSL does not have.

props.title: Four Questions, Four Lines
props.status: THE ASSIGNMENT'S FOUR QUESTIONS — each answer points at a line
props.source: Source: game/shaders/invulnerable_tint.gdshader line 8; godot/materials/circle_darkstone.tres line 9; godot/shaders/weathered_stone.gdshader lines 4 and 7.

beats.narration_text: The specification came first. The brief was committed before either shader existed, and it holds the colour line: mix the incoming colour toward the tint colour, by tint amount times tint strength. The strength is point four, not more: at point six the heart's outline would fall to two point one to one against the sky, under the three to one the brief requires. It also fixes the timing: the tint shows for one point one eight three seconds, plus or minus one frame, at thirty, sixty and a hundred and forty-four frames a second. Claude drafted it, and shuai-z reviewed it.

props.title: The Colour Line, Specified First
props.status: CHANGE-BRIEF.md · revision 1, committed before either shader existed
props.source: Source: CHANGE-BRIEF.md §2 (fc9cd523; the shader came later, ae0a3757). Drafted by Claude, reviewed by shuai-z.

beats.narration_text: This is the shader, nine lines, typed by shuai-z from the brief. Shader type canvas item makes it a 2D shader. Three uniforms: tint amount, which the game drives, and the colour and the strength, which only the material sets. Then the answer to the first question. A shader is a small program the GPU runs for every fragment it draws, and here fragment runs once for each fragment of the hearts. COLOR arrives already holding the heart's texel times its modulate, and line eight moves only its red, green and blue toward the pale blue. Alpha is never written, so transparent pixels stay transparent.

beats.narration_text: And this is what line eight does, in a window, in the Compatibility renderer. A scripted run stopped the driver and set tint amount from code: zero, a half, one, and two. The full heart's red is two hundred, sixty-four, fifty-three at zero, and a hundred and eighty-one, one twenty-eight, one thirty-four at one: exactly the brief's prediction, and the half matches too. Inside the empty heart, where alpha is zero, the sky stays the same at every value. At two, the red lands one step from the unclamped prediction and eighty-one steps from the clamped one. So hint range shapes the Inspector's slider. It does not clamp a value set from code.

shot.observation: Windowed Compatibility captures with the driver stopped and tint_amount set from code to 0.0, 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0: P1 and P2 equal the brief's predictions at 0.0, 0.5 and 1.0; at 2.0 P1 is one step off the unclamped prediction and 81 from the clamped one; P3 stays the sky.

beats.narration_text: The driver is one line in the HUD script, and it runs every frame. It divides Rudy's invulnerable time left by the window's length, and sets that as tint amount on the hearts' material. It reads his state and never writes it. That is half of the second answer, too. The shader file holds the default, zero. The material, hearts tint dot t r e s, holds the current value, and it is local to the scene, so no other node shares it.

props.title: One Line Drives It
props.source: Source: assignment-5/game/ui/hud.gd, lines 108–111 (verbatim). Godot editor reconstruction.
props.code:
## The hearts take on the lit waystone's glow while Rudy is invulnerable,
## fading with the time left (CHANGE-BRIEF.md). Reads his state, never sets it.
func _tint_hearts() -> void:
	(_hearts.material as ShaderMaterial).set_shader_parameter(&"tint_amount", _rudy._invulnerable_left / _rudy.invulnerable_time)
output: rudy.gd is unchanged byte for byte; the driver reads _invulnerable_left and invulnerable_time

beats.narration_text: Now the 3D side, and the third question: why is a texture information? These are Rock 01's three maps, from Poly Haven, by Rob Tuytel, C C zero. Only the first is a colour. The normal map stores the direction each bit of surface faces, in its red and green; the roughness map stores how sharp a reflection is. Those are numbers, not colours, so they must not be decoded as sRGB, and every import setting is set explicitly, so the editor has nothing left to change. A curl check, calibrated on the OpenGL and DirectX pair, confirmed the normal map's convention: point one four four, against one point eight six.

props.title: Three Maps, One Colour
props.status: ROCK 01 · Poly Haven · Rob Tuytel · CC0 — the 1k PNGs as committed
props.source: Source: godot/assets/textures/rock_01/ and ATTRIBUTION.md (https://polyhaven.com/a/rock_01); import settings in each .import file; curl ratios: logs/godot_calibrate_normal_map_check_60fps.log. The 16-bit roughness map is shown scaled to 8 bits.

beats.narration_text: This is that interface swept, captured in a window under the scene's own light. Claude did this check at shuai-z's request, and shuai-z reviewed it. Albedo tint at black takes away the photo's colour. U V scale breaks the look at both ends: at a quarter the texels blur, and at four the grain is too fine to read. Normal strength and roughness offset barely move it, under three steps on average. The normal map is gentle, the roughness map is nearly flat, and the sun's highlight cannot land on the stone's sides. The numbers show both uniforms reach the shader. Under this light, an eye cannot judge them.

shot.observation: Close-up windowed captures under the scene's own lighting, each uniform at min, default and max on the loaded material: albedo_tint black 73.51 steps; uv_scale 0.25 12.51 and 4.0 9.20; normal_strength 2.62 and 2.93; roughness_offset 2.64 and 0.90 (mean largest-channel change).

beats.narration_text: And here it is running: the real props scene, in Forward Plus, at 4K. Only the camera moves, on a film-only script on a copy; the props, the light and both materials are as saved. Once around the scene. The waystone's stone and the circle's dark disc are drawn by this shader, through their own materials, while the rune, the moss, the spikes and the gold keep their flat imported colours. Then close to the waystone: the grain is the photo's, lit by the scene's one sun. And over the circle. Its material makes the disc darker, flatter in relief and glossier: three values, on the same shader.

beats.narration_text: The test, in memory and never saved. The two materials share one shader object. Halve ALBEDO in line eighteen of the loaded shader, and both stones darken: by twenty-two and a half steps, and by ten and a half. Change one value in the circle's material, its tint to white, and only the circle changes, by twenty steps; the waystone by zero. The first try, normal strength at two, moved the circle by less than a step, too little to see, so the check was revised to the tint.

beats.narration_text: For comparison, shuai-z converted a standard material with the same textures into shader code in the editor, and annotated it. Two of its lines, beside mine. Its albedo sampler says source color, as mine does on line three. Its normal goes to NORMAL MAP, with the strength set apart on NORMAL MAP DEPTH, as my lines nineteen and twenty do. But its normal hint is hint roughness normal, not hint normal. And the generated file has sixteen uniforms; mine has seven.

shot.observation: Verbatim lines from standard_generated.gdshader (10–11, 69–72, with shuai-z's comments) above their equivalents in weathered_stone.gdshader (3–4, 19–20).

beats.narration_text: Now what the tests proved. This is the duration check in the driver's test. The test plays through real input and samples tint amount once a frame. Here it measures how long the tint shows, from its first frame to its last: seventy-one sixtieths of a second, plus or minus one frame, and two point four seconds of real time at half speed. The test never calls take hit, and never sets the shader parameter itself.

props.title: Measuring the Window
props.code:
for label: String in ["hit 1", "hit 2 (time scale 0.5)"]:
		var w: Dictionary = labelled[label]
		var expected := 71.0 / 60.0 if label == "hit 1" else 144.0 / 60.0
		var span := float(w.end - w.first) / _fps if not w.is_empty() and w.end >= 0 else INF
		spans_ok = spans_ok and absf(span - expected) <= 1.0 / _fps + EPS
		spans.append("%s %.4f s of real time, expected %.4f s ± %.4f" % [label, span, expected, 1.0 / _fps])
	_check("A9 the tint shows for 1.183 s ± one frame at time scale 1.0, and for 2.4 s of real time ± one frame at 0.5",
		spans_ok, ", ".join(spans))

beats.narration_text: Headless output, at three pinned frame rates, through the course's wrapper. One point two, one point one eight three three, and one point one eight oh six seconds, each within one frame of the prediction. Fifteen of fifteen checks at every rate. In the driver's own session, a frame-counting version of the HUD failed this check at thirty and at a hundred and forty-four. But these are numbers about what the material holds, not about a single pixel.

shot.observation: Recorded headless output at 30, 60 and 144 fps through scripts/run-test.sh: 15 PASS and 'all checks passed' at each; A9 1.2000, 1.1833 and 1.1806 s against 1.1833 ± one frame, and 2.4 s at time scale 0.5; A10 no rise; A11 the respawn's jump; A12 the pause holds.

beats.narration_text: Can the checks fail? shuai-z made three mutations. Delete the semicolon after shader type, and there is a shader error, and the test exits with one. Rename tint amount: the shader still parses, so only the uniform check catches it, and it exits with one. Delete source color from the albedo sampler: no error at all, but the materials test reads the hint from the source, fails one check, and exits with one. Clean, that test passes a hundred and twenty-five of a hundred and twenty-five, after a fresh import from an empty cache.

shot.observation: Recorded headless output of the three mutations shuai-z made: no semicolon (SHADER ERROR, 2 failed), tint_amount renamed (2 failed, no shader error), source_color deleted from albedo_tex (1 failed); and test_materials.gd at 125 PASS.

beats.narration_text: And what no headless run can show. The headless renderer draws nothing, so every look in this film comes from a window. Even then, which picture you trust matters. A macOS screenshot of the hint scene reads four to eleven steps darker than the engine's own capture, because it carries the display's colour profile; converted to sRGB, it matches exactly. And no test can say the hearts read well, or that the stone looks like stone. Those were eyes: shuai-z played the game, watched the fade-in, and checked the materials in the editor.

shot.observation: The hint scene's engine capture beside a macOS screenshot of the same window: the screenshot reads 4 to 11 steps darker in every band; converted from the display profile to sRGB it matches the engine exactly.

beats.narration_text: Verdict. Checked by machine: the existing hundred and forty-one and forty-four checks still pass; the tint test passes at three frame rates; the materials test passes after a fresh import; and three mutations each fail. In windowed captures, the hearts at zero, a half and one, and all six hint bands, match the predictions exactly. By eye, shuai-z played it, including the three edge cases. Uncertain: why the hearts need no sRGB step is read from the engine's source, not checked here; one edge pixel is one step off, unexplained; two stone controls cannot be judged under this light; and nobody else has played it. The agents' mistakes that were caught: a probe that counted its own marker as a shader error; permission rules that stopped matching after a change of folder; Rock 01 copied to the wrong folder, which the first import showed; and an audit's three megabytes that nobody measured.

artifactLines: Machine: 141/141 and 44/44 existing checks; the tint test 15/15 at 30, 60 and 144 fps; test_materials 125/125 after a fresh import; three mutations each exit 1.

Windowed captures: hearts P1/P2 exact at 0.0, 0.5, 1.0; six hint bands exact. Eyes: shuai-z played: tint, fade-in, back on the spikes, last heart, pause. Sweep and two materials: Claude, at shuai-z's request; reviewed.

beats.act: verdict — who made what, next step
beats.narration_text: Who made what. shuai-z wrote the three shaders and committed each alone, reviewed the brief and every prompt, made the mutations, chose the circle's tint and the curl threshold, annotated the generated shader, wrote the language notes, and played the game. Claude drafted the brief and the records, ran the scoped sessions that wrote the driver, its test and the materials audit, wrote the capture tools, did the sweep at shuai-z's request, and made this film. The textures are Rock 01, by Rob Tuytel, C C zero. The source shown is a two a three a seven seven. The next step: a test scene with a low, grazing light, so normal strength and roughness offset can be judged by eye.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt; read it with me. Read my change brief and the hearts' tint shader. Then, on a copy, set the strength to point six in the hearts' material, not the shader, run the tint capture, and show me the pixels beside my prediction. Write your prediction down first.
